h1:
Hat Yai for Cross-Border Shoppers
A Shop-and-Eat Route from Sadao/Padang Besar
intro: Hat Yai is the town Malaysians and Singaporeans have been driving or taking the train across the border to shop in for decades. Nuts, snacks, cosmetics, and food all run noticeably cheaper than back home, and the food is good enough that you'll want to carry some back with you. This article maps out a 2-day, 1-night route built specifically for people entering via the Sadao border (Dannok) or Padang Besar — where to start, which shopping district to hit first, where to change money at a good rate, and where to stash your souvenirs so you're not lugging bags around all day.

blocks.html: If you're coming to Hat Yai from Malaysia or Singapore specifically to shop, the list is usually clear: nuts and cashews, imported snacks, cosmetics, clothes, sarongs, and eating well at every meal. The town is compact enough that you can do most of your shopping in one district on foot, but get the order wrong and you'll spend the whole day hauling heavy bags. So we've planned it to buy the heavy stuff last and space the food out across the day.

blocks.text: Which way into Hat Yai — Sadao vs Padang Besar

blocks.html: Shoppers from Malaysia have two main ways into Hat Yai, each suited to a different traveler. Pick based on whether you're coming by private car, by train, or on a tour bus.

items: Sadao border (Dannok / Bukit Kayu Hitam) — Songkhla's busiest road crossing, about 58 km from Hat Yai, roughly a 1-hour drive or minivan ride. Best for people arriving by private car or tour bus. The Thai side runs about 05:00–23:00; leave extra time on long weekends, since the queue at the border can drag on.

Padang Besar — Best for people coming by train from Penang/Butterworth. You take the train on the Malaysian side, walk across the border, and board the Thai train at Padang Besar station on the Thai side into Hat Yai Junction. It takes about 45 minutes and costs around 50 THB, with only a few departures a day, so check the schedule ahead.

Minivan/bus — Minivans run Hat Yai–Sadao–Dannok and Hat Yai–Padang Besar all day, with fares in the tens of THB. You can catch them near the bus terminal beside Central Festival Hat Yai. The last return departures leave in the afternoon to early evening, so don't push it too late.

blocks.title: Allow time at the border
blocks.html: On Fridays through Sundays and Malaysian long weekends, the car queue at the Sadao border gets very long. Cross late in the morning and you may not reach Hat Yai until afternoon. Leave the Malaysian side early so you get a full first day of shopping.

blocks.text: Where to change ringgit for a good rate

blocks.html: Hat Yai has over 70 money-changers, clustered around the Niphat Uthit streets and near Kim Yong Market. Big chains like Kin-Exchange, K79, and K81 are popular because their rates are steady and they're open every day. Compare 2–3 shops before you change — they usually differ a little. Shops in the market and around town already take ringgit and Singapore dollars, but paying in Thai baht gets you a better deal than handing over ringgit directly almost everywhere.

items: Changing in Hat Yai beats changing at the border — exchange counters at the border or duty free usually can't match in-town rates. Just change enough for your first stretch of spending.
Carry baht cash for the markets — Kim Yong, Santisuk, and most souvenir stalls take cash, and paying in baht gets a better price and easier bargaining.
Big malls take cards — Central and Lee Garden accept foreign cards, so keep a card for bigger items, cosmetics, and brand-name goods.

blocks.text: Hat Yai's main shopping districts, before you dive in

items.name: Kim Yong Market
items.blurb: A two-floor indoor market and the symbol of Hat Yai, selling nuts, cashews, dried fruit, and imported snacks from Malaysia/Singapore/China — souvenirs all in one place. Open roughly 07:00–19:00.

items.name: Santisuk Market
items.blurb: Right next to Kim Yong, focused on clothing, sarongs, garments, and dry goods. You can walk straight over from Kim Yong on the same trip.

items.name: Lee Garden Plaza
items.blurb: A busy downtown mall with clothing, cosmetics, and restaurants, an easy walk to Kim Yong Market. A handy meet-up point in the center of town.

items.name: Central Hat Yai
items.blurb: A big air-conditioned mall with Central, Tops, B2S, Supersports, a cinema, and an ice rink. The lower floor has plenty of halal food. Good for escaping the afternoon heat.

items.name: ASEAN Night Bazaar
items.blurb: A night market with street food, clothes, and toys at easy prices, and a lively atmosphere after dark.

items.name: Greenway Market
items.blurb: An evening market with a varied food court and all kinds of odds and ends. Open Tuesday–Saturday, roughly 17:00–22:00.

blocks.title: Shop in a smart order
blocks.html: Save the heavy stuff — nuts, snacks, drinks — for the end, just before heading back to your hotel or out of town. Don't buy it first thing in the morning and carry it all day. Many shops in Kim Yong will hold your purchases or deliver them to your in-town hotel, so ask before you pay.

This is built for arriving in Hat Yai in the morning to midday on day one, staying one night downtown, then buying the heavy souvenirs before heading back on day two. Adjust the timing for whenever you reach town.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Into town, wander downtown, hit the night bazaar

items.activity: Arrive in Hat Yai, check in to a downtown hotel around Niphat Uthit / near Lee Garden
items.note: Pick a hotel within walking distance of Kim Yong so it's easy to drop off souvenirs.

items.activity: Change money at a big-chain shop around Niphat Uthit, then grab lunch
items.note: Try Hat Yai dim sum or chicken rice — these places are mostly open morning to midday.

items.activity: Walk Lee Garden Plaza out of the sun, browse clothes and cosmetics
items.note: Mall prices are steady, good for comparing before you bargain at the markets.

items.activity: Rest your legs at a downtown cafe before the evening
items.note: Hat Yai has loads of cafes — pick one near your hotel for an easy walk back.

items.activity: Head to the ASEAN Night Bazaar or Greenway for street food dinner
items.note: Greenway runs Tuesday–Saturday 17:00–22:00; if you're here on Sunday/Monday, go to the night bazaar instead.

items.activity: Browse snacks, toys, and cheap clothes at the evening market
items.note: Buy the light stuff tonight; leave the heavy stuff for tomorrow.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Tackle Kim Yong–Santisuk, grab souvenirs before heading back

items.activity: Hat Yai-style breakfast — congee, dim sum, or old-school coffee
items.note: Morning shops open early and sell out fast, so go before mid-morning to get the full spread.

items.activity: Work through Kim Yong Market — pick nuts, cashews, imported snacks
items.note: It's quieter and cooler early, and easier to bargain than later in the morning.

items.activity: Walk over to Santisuk Market for sarongs, clothes, and dry goods
items.note: It's right next to Kim Yong, so you can carry straight on in one trip.

items.activity: A closing lunch — try bold southern Thai dishes or halal food at Central
items.note: Central's lower floor has plenty of halal food, good for Muslim travelers.

items.activity: Back to the hotel to gather your souvenirs, pack, and separate the heavy stuff
items.note: If you left purchases at a Kim Yong shop, pick them up now or have them delivered to the hotel.

items.activity: Catch the minivan/train back to Sadao or Padang Besar
items.note: Check the last departure carefully — return minivans/trains often run out in the evening, and allow for the border queue too.

blocks.text: What cross-border shoppers carry back + rough prices

items: Cashews — a southern specialty; around 400 THB/kg at Kim Yong. Pick a vendor that lets you taste first.
Nuts and macadamias — macadamias around 380 THB/kg, pistachios around 440 THB/kg, sweet crunchy almonds around 540 THB/kg.
Imported Malaysian/Singaporean/Chinese snacks — some are cheaper at Kim Yong than back home.
Dried fruit and local sweets — mango leather, durian paste, and mooncake-style pastries make light souvenirs.
Cosmetics/skincare — often cheaper in Thailand; buy at Central or Lee Garden to be sure they're genuine.
Clothes and sarongs — Santisuk and the markets around Kim Yong have plenty to choose from at easy prices.

blocks.title: Bargain politely
blocks.html: You can haggle at the markets, but ask nicely and buy in bulk for a better price. Many shops throw in extras when you buy a lot. Feel free to mention you're visiting from Malaysia/Singapore — vendors are used to cross-border customers.

items: Passport and border hours — check the opening times on both sides; it's crowded on long weekends, so leave enough time to cross in and out.
Bring-back quotas for Malaysia — some goods have import limits on the Malaysian side, so check customs rules before you carry a lot.
SIM or roaming — buy a Thai SIM at the border or in town for maps, ride-hailing, and price-comparing.
Keep baht cash on hand — markets and minivans mostly take cash, so don't rely on cards alone.

faq.q: Is it better to enter Hat Yai via Sadao or Padang Besar?
faq.a: If you're coming by private car or tour bus, the Sadao border (Dannok) is more convenient — about 58 km from Hat Yai, roughly a 1-hour drive. If you're coming by train from Penang, enter via Padang Besar and connect to the Thai train into Hat Yai Junction, about 45 minutes. Pick based on how you're traveling.

faq.q: Where in Hat Yai is the cheapest, most complete place for souvenirs?
faq.a: Kim Yong Market is the main spot for cross-border shoppers, with nuts, cashews, imported snacks, and dried fruit all in one place. Walk over to the adjacent Santisuk Market for clothes and sarongs. Go early — it's quieter and easier to bargain.

faq.q: Where in Hat Yai can I change ringgit at a good rate?
faq.a: Hat Yai has over 70 money-changers around Niphat Uthit and near Kim Yong Market. Big chains like Kin-Exchange, K79, and K81 have steady rates and open every day. Changing in town beats the border, and it's worth comparing 2–3 shops first.

faq.q: How many days do I need to shop Hat Yai?
faq.a: Two days and one night is about right for shoppers — downtown malls and the night bazaar on day one, then Kim Yong–Santisuk for souvenirs before heading back on day two. If you're really short on time, you can cover Kim Yong and Lee Garden in a single day.

faq.q: Roughly how much do Hat Yai souvenirs cost?
faq.a: At Kim Yong, cashews run around 400 THB/kg, macadamias around 380 THB/kg, pistachios around 440 THB/kg, and sweet crunchy almonds around 540 THB/kg. Buy in bulk and you usually get a better price plus a little something thrown in.
